questions.prompt: Olbers' paradox, as Keating frames it, asks why:
choices: B The night sky is dark if the universe were infinite, static, and filled with stars.
questions.explain: A dark night sky is paradoxical under naive infinite-static-star assumptions.

questions.prompt: Edwin Hubble, using Leavitt's Cepheid work, concluded roughly that galaxies' recession relates to:
choices: A Random blueshifts equally at all distances.
B A distance–redshift/velocity relation (Hubble's law) tracing expansion.
questions.explain: Hubble combined Cepheid distances with redshifts to reveal expansion.

questions.prompt: What are the units of the Hubble constant as Keating discusses them?
choices: B Kilometers per second per megaparsec.
questions.explain: He stresses km/s/Mpc units and their inverse-time implication.

questions.prompt: Running cosmic expansion backward, Keating says, suggests:
choices: A An eternal unchanging crystal sphere.
B A time when matter was compressed together—supporting the Big Bang picture.
C Instant creation of only Earth.
questions.explain: Backward extrapolation is a pillar of the Big Bang model.

questions.prompt: What early-universe spark theory does Keating mention (and link to his book Losing the Nobel Prize)?
choices: A Steady-state creation of galaxies forever only.
questions.explain: He discusses cosmic inflation as the conjectured early expansion spark.
